about.title: From code to architecture
about.p1: I'm a software engineer with a solution-architecture background, at Minsait. For over a year I've been on SIMPL-Open, the European Commission's open-source middleware for data spaces, defining and reviewing API-first contracts (OpenAPI), data models and integration architecture with international teams. I also build internal tooling with AI agents (Spec-Driven Development, coding agents, MCP) and automate with GitHub Actions.
about.p2: Before that I automated banking test suites at NTT DATA, and I'm now doing my master's in Computer Engineering at Universidad de Sevilla alongside the job. I care about understanding why a tool works, not just how to use it. And that coffee is mine.

projects.faro.title: Faro — a copilot for Jira and Confluence
projects.faro.desc: Chrome extension that turns a local opencode server into a copilot inside Jira and Confluence: it answers, walks you to the page by unfolding the tree and highlights the exact passage.
projects.faro.method: Built with Spec-Driven Development and AI-assisted development.
projects.faro.facts: 13 milestones · 13 adversarial reviews · 145 findings applied · 1,283 dependency-free tests
projects.faro.alt: Mock of Faro's side panel next to a Confluence page with a highlighted passage and a numbered badge
projects.paper.title: Evaluating the Incremental Contribution of Chest X-⁠ray to 24-⁠Hour ICU Deterioration Prediction
projects.paper.authors: Marco Tenorio Cortés, Andreea Madalina Oprescu and María del Carmen Romero Ternero
projects.paper.venue: To be presented at CAEPIA 2026 in Jaén, Spain: Wednesday 11 November, 11:00 to 12:30, in session SG 3 · Computer vision and robotics.
projects.paper.note: Day and time as listed in the conference's provisional programme.
projects.paper.badge: In press · full text with the proceedings
projects.paper.alt: Two pages of a scientific paper with the title, the authors, a figure showing a chest X-ray and the CAEPIA 2026 Jaén seal
projects.faro.detail.lead: A Chrome side panel powered by the opencode running on your own machine. It answers questions about Jira and Confluence with the model you choose, guides you down the page tree to the right page and marks the passage it is talking about. Local and read-only.
projects.faro.detail.context: On a large project, documentation is spread across thousands of pages and issues, and finding the paragraph that settles a question takes longer than the question itself. A generic assistant answers, but it doesn't say where it's written. Faro exists for that: every answer comes with its place, and the place can be checked.
projects.faro.detail.role1: I designed and built the whole extension: side panel, content scripts, service worker and an opencode client over HTTP and SSE, as ES modules with no build step.
projects.faro.detail.role2: I made the route to each page come from the site's real page tree, not from the model: it is read from the REST API with your session, and the browser navigates only once.
projects.faro.detail.role3: I built Analysis mode: the model sees the page as numbered blocks, and a script, not the model, decides which passage each finding underlines.
projects.faro.detail.role4: I shut the door on prompt injection: whatever comes from a page is information, the model never emits URLs and opencode denies everything except the MCP.
projects.faro.detail.cycle_text: I built it with Spec-Driven Development and AI agents: a CLAUDE.md acts as the living spec, and all thirteen milestones followed the same cycle, never moving on until the review was closed.
projects.faro.detail.cycle_alt: The cycle of every milestone around CLAUDE.md, the living spec: pure module with its test, wiring, visual test bench, documentation and adversarial review, then round again for the next milestone.
projects.faro.detail.arch_intro: Five parts and one rule: only the panel talks to opencode. The content script lives inside Jira or Confluence, on a page it doesn't control, and only carries out orders that have already been validated.
projects.faro.detail.diagram_alt: Faro's architecture: in Chrome, the Jira or Confluence page with its content script and the side panel; the panel talks to opencode on your machine, which reasons with an LLM and queries Atlassian through a read-only MCP; the route through the page tree is read from the site's REST API with your session.
projects.faro.detail.flow1: You ask in the panel; the page travels as numbered blocks, labelled as information and never as instructions.
projects.faro.detail.flow2: The panel sends the turn to opencode on your machine over password-protected HTTP, and the answer streams back over SSE.
projects.faro.detail.flow3: opencode reasons with the model you choose and queries Jira and Confluence through MCP, read-only.
projects.faro.detail.flow4: The route to the page isn't invented by the model: it comes from the site's REST API, with your session and GET only.
projects.faro.detail.flow5: The answer carries identifiers, not URLs: the panel checks them against the index, and the content script unfolds the tree, navigates once and underlines.
projects.faro.detail.result1: 1,283 unit tests on a home-grown, dependency-free harness, plus integration tests against a real opencode and a visual test bench.
projects.faro.detail.result2: Prompts for 37 scenarios are compared byte by byte with their snapshots: no change slips through unseen.
projects.faro.detail.result3: A WCAG 2.1 contrast test for every colour pair, and a check that fails when the documentation drifts from the code.
projects.faro.detail.learned: That with AI the bottleneck is no longer writing code but specifying and verifying. What worked was treating every decision as a written contract and not trusting what the model claims: routes, anchors and links are decided by a script.
projects.simpl.detail.lead: The open-source middleware the European Commission is building so that public and private organisations can share data, applications and infrastructure in data spaces, with trust and without vendor lock-in. For over a year I've been on its architecture team (PSO), defining and reviewing API-first contracts, data models and integration flows with international teams.
projects.simpl.detail.context: A data space brings together participants who neither know nor trust each other by default: someone has to settle who is who, what is on offer, on what terms and how it is checked. SIMPL-Open provides that common layer so each sector can build its own on top, and every organisation joins by running its own agent.
projects.simpl.detail.role1: I define and review API-first REST APIs: OpenAPI 3 contracts, schemas (allOf/anyOf), versioning, OAuth 2.0/OIDC and RFC 9457 errors, following the programme's API guidelines and Belgif; every change verified against its epic and acceptance criteria in Jira.
projects.simpl.detail.role2: I review the Common Data Models and the consistency between functional requirements, integration contracts and architecture docs, and I've proposed automating that validation in CI.
projects.simpl.detail.role3: I work on the data-space integration flows: identity and access (Tier 1/2, JWT, RBAC/ABAC, mTLS/X.509), federated catalogues, EDC connectors and data exchange and integration (ETL) flows.
projects.simpl.detail.role4: I coordinate technically in English: findings and follow-up in Jira/Confluence, minutes of the architecture meetings, and cross-team blockers and dependencies.
projects.simpl.detail.arch_intro: Each participant runs an agent with two doors. Its users come in through Tier 1, which is private and role-based (RBAC); agents talk to each other through Tier 2, the only exposed one, over mutual TLS with attribute-based control (ABAC). The governance authority, one per data space, onboards participants and hosts the catalogue.
projects.simpl.detail.diagram_alt: A data space with SIMPL-Open: at the top, the governance authority with onboarding, identity and the catalogue; below, the consumer's and the provider's agents, each with its Tier 1 and Tier 2; between them, over mutual TLS, contract negotiation and transfer. The interfaces between agents and with the catalogue, in blue, are OpenAPI contracts.
projects.simpl.detail.step1: Onboarding: the governance authority vets the participant and issues its identity, an X.509 certificate carrying its attributes.
projects.simpl.detail.step2: Publishing: the provider describes its resource with DCAT-AP metadata and publishes it to the catalogue.
projects.simpl.detail.step3: Discovery: the consumer searches the catalogue from its own agent.
projects.simpl.detail.step4: Negotiation: the agents authenticate each other over mutual TLS, the provider applies its policies to the consumer's attributes and a contract is agreed.
projects.simpl.detail.step5: Transfer: the data plane delivers the resource under the agreed terms.
projects.simpl.detail.caption: In blue, the interfaces backed by an OpenAPI contract: the part of the system I design and review.
projects.simpl.detail.stack1: OpenAPI 3, reviewed against the programme's API guidelines and Belgif (RFC 9457 errors)
projects.simpl.detail.stack3: Dataspace Protocol: catalogue, contract negotiation and transfer
projects.simpl.detail.stack4: X.509 certificates with attributes and mutual TLS between agents
projects.simpl.detail.stack5: DCAT-AP to describe data, applications and infrastructure
projects.simpl.detail.learned: That in a federated system the architecture lives in the contracts. One ambiguous field in an OpenAPI spec turns into three interpretations in three teams, so reviewing an API is mostly reviewing an agreement: names, errors, versions and what happens when something fails.
projects.qa.detail.lead: Automated testing for banking at NTT DATA, plus a public framework that simulates a bank's API, with a Spring Boot REST API and Gherkin scenarios.
projects.qa.detail.fact4_label: in a cookie, behind a filter
projects.qa.detail.context: In banking, a failed transfer is never a minor detail. At NTT DATA I automated tests for the banking sector, first as an intern and then as a junior QA tester. The framework is a team project with a teaching goal: a simulated bank for learning API testing.
projects.qa.detail.role1: I designed and ran automated tests for banking with Selenium, JUnit and Cucumber, to the quality standards of the financial sector.
projects.qa.detail.role2: With the framework team we built the REST API in Java and Spring Boot: customers, accounts, cards and transfers on in-memory H2.
projects.qa.detail.role3: We secured it with JWT: login leaves the token in a cookie, and a filter answers 401 to any request without a session, except for /public routes.
projects.qa.detail.role4: We wrote the tests in Gherkin with Cucumber and JUnit 5, with steps grouped by controller and a shared context.
projects.qa.detail.arch_intro: A Maven project with two halves: the bank, and the framework that walks through it like a customer. The suite starts Spring Boot and talks to the API over HTTP through BankAPI, a Java interface with every endpoint.
projects.qa.detail.diagram_alt: Architecture of the test framework. On the left, the framework: a Gherkin .feature file, steps grouped by controller with their shared TestContext, an @After hook that cleans up, and the BankAPI client, which sends requests over HTTP to the bank's API. The Spring Boot API goes through a JWT filter, controllers, services and repositories down to an in-memory H2 database. Below, GitHub Actions runs mvn clean test on every push and publishes the Cucumber report as HTML and PDF.
projects.qa.detail.caption: In blue, what every request goes through: the BankAPI client and the JWT filter.
projects.qa.detail.step1: A Gherkin scenario describes the case with examples: sign up with N accounts and M cards, log in and check the cards.
projects.qa.detail.step2: Each step lives in its controller's file and leaves its data in the TestContext for the next one.
projects.qa.detail.step3: BankAPI sends the request over HTTP with the login cookie.
projects.qa.detail.step4: The API validates the JWT and goes down through controller, service and repository to H2; the step checks the response.
projects.qa.detail.step5: When each scenario ends, an @After hook deletes what it created and resets the context.
projects.qa.detail.step6: On every push to main, GitHub Actions runs the suite and commits the Cucumber report to the repository as HTML and PDF.
projects.qa.detail.learned: That a test is worth what you understand by reading it. Gherkin makes you name every step the way the business would, and splitting steps across files taught me that a suite's shared state is designed from the start, not discovered when it breaks.
projects.tfg.detail.lead: An autoencoder that has only ever seen benign tumours and flags whatever it can't reconstruct. It is my bachelor's thesis in Computer Engineering, on the Breast Cancer Wisconsin dataset, with a Flask web demo.
projects.tfg.detail.context: When almost every sample is benign, a malignant tumour behaves like an anomaly, and a classifier that has barely seen malignant cases learns to say everything is fine. The thesis turns this around: teach the model only what normal looks like and measure how hard each sample is to reconstruct.
projects.tfg.detail.role1: I prepared the data: dropped a redundant feature after studying the correlations and cut malignant samples down to 10% of the benign ones to recreate an anomaly scenario.
projects.tfg.detail.role2: I designed the autoencoder in Keras, from 29 down to 8 neurons and back, with L1 regularisation, Adam, MSE loss and early stopping, and tuned its hyperparameters.
projects.tfg.detail.role3: I chose the threshold with precision–recall and ROC curves, and compared against KNN, a decision tree and a random forest.
projects.tfg.detail.role4: I built a Flask demo that takes a form or an Excel file and returns benign or malignant for each sample.
projects.tfg.detail.arch_intro: The model squeezes each sample down to 8 values and expands it again. Since it has only learned what a benign tumour looks like, anything unlike it comes back worse, and that error decides.
projects.tfg.detail.diagram_alt: Autoencoder for anomaly detection: six layers of 29, 16, 8, 8, 16 and 29 neurons, with the 8-neuron bottleneck in the middle. The original input and its reconstruction are compared with the mean squared error; if the error exceeds the threshold the sample is an anomaly, a likely malignant tumour, otherwise benign. Below, the Flask demo: a form or an Excel file goes through the saved scaler and model and returns a verdict.
projects.tfg.detail.caption: One dot per neuron. In blue, the bottleneck and the error that decides.
projects.tfg.detail.step1: Input: 29 measurements per sample (radius, texture, perimeter…), scaled with a StandardScaler fitted on benign samples.
projects.tfg.detail.step2: The encoder compresses them from 29 to 8 and the decoder tries to rebuild them.
projects.tfg.detail.step3: The reconstruction error is the mean squared error between the input and its reconstruction.
projects.tfg.detail.step4: If it exceeds the threshold, the sample is an anomaly, a likely malignant tumour; otherwise, benign.
projects.tfg.detail.step5: The demo follows the same path with the saved model and scaler.
projects.tfg.detail.result1: On the notebook's test split, the autoencoder catches 9 of the 11 malignant samples with a single false alarm among 68 benign ones.
projects.tfg.detail.result2: KNN, a decision tree and a random forest, trained the same way on benign samples only, label everything benign.
projects.tfg.detail.learned: That in an imbalanced problem the question matters as much as the algorithm. Swapping “is it malignant?” for “does it look benign?” is what made the model useful, and the threshold turned out to be as delicate a decision as the architecture.
projects.cinema.detail.lead: A website for booking cinema tickets: films now showing, upcoming releases, screenings by day and a seat map for picking your seat. It is the final project of Harvard's CS50's Web Programming with Python and JavaScript, built with Django, SQLite and JavaScript.
projects.cinema.detail.fact2_label: seats per screening, A1 to E10
projects.cinema.detail.fact4_label: course projects in the same repository
projects.cinema.detail.context: CS50 Web teaches Django, SQL and JavaScript with one project per topic: search, wiki, auctions, email and a social network, all in the same repository. The final one is open, and a cinema is a good modelling exercise: every film has its screenings, every screening its seats, and no seat is sold twice.
projects.cinema.detail.role1: I modelled the data with Django's ORM: users, genres, films, screenings and tickets, where each ticket ties a user to a screening and a seat.
projects.cinema.detail.role2: I made each film decide on its own whether it is showing: on save it compares its release date with today, and the rest go to “Upcoming”.
projects.cinema.detail.role3: I wrote the seat map in JavaScript: taken seats blocked, two wheelchair spaces and multi-seat selection.
projects.cinema.detail.role4: I added “My tickets”, with refunds without reloading the page, and a script that loads the films with five screenings each.
projects.cinema.detail.arch_intro: A classic Django app: views rendering templates on top of SQLite, and JavaScript only where it's needed, in the seat map and in refunds.
projects.cinema.detail.diagram_alt: Booking flow and data model of Cinema. At the top, the four screens of a booking: films now showing, the day's screenings, the seat map with 5 rows of 10 seats, and “My tickets”, with the option to refund. Below, the five models: Genre and Movie in a many-to-many relation, each Movie with its Screenings, each Screening with its Tickets, and each Ticket belonging to a User.
projects.cinema.detail.caption: In blue, the ticket: it ties a user to a screening and a seat.
projects.cinema.detail.step1: Now showing: the home page lists released films with their genres, and upcoming releases have their own page.
projects.cinema.detail.step2: Screenings: pick a day and see each showing with its time and auditorium.
projects.cinema.detail.step3: Seats: the map marks taken seats and wheelchair spaces; buying requires logging in.
projects.cinema.detail.step4: Ticket: after a simulated payment, the server checks each seat again and creates one ticket per seat, which can be refunded.
projects.cinema.detail.stack1: Django: views, templates, authentication and ORM
projects.cinema.detail.stack2: SQLite; film data from the OMDb API
projects.cinema.detail.learned: That a good data model does half the work. With the screening and the seat on every ticket, finding free seats is a single query, and the rule that matters, never selling the same seat twice, is checked on the server even though the interface already prevents it.
projects.nakoa.detail.lead: A multiplayer game built in Unity with one clear goal: the same game running on a phone, a computer and a browser. A single C# project that builds for Android, iOS, PC and WebGL.
projects.nakoa.detail.fact2_label: desktop systems: Windows, macOS and Linux
projects.nakoa.detail.fact3_label: Unity project for all of them
projects.nakoa.detail.fact4_label: in the demo, with WebGL 1 as a fallback
projects.nakoa.detail.context: The idea was to let every player choose where to play: on a phone, on a computer or in the browser, with nothing to install. Nakoa started from that premise: not four games, but a single one that builds for each device and plays just as well on all of them.
projects.nakoa.detail.role1: I built the game in Unity with C#, as a single project ready to build for Android, iOS, PC and WebGL.
projects.nakoa.detail.role2: I kept what is shared apart from what depends on the device: scenes, logic and assets are common, while input and UI adapt to each platform.
projects.nakoa.detail.role3: I published a WebGL build on GitHub Pages as a playable demo: it runs in the browser with WebAssembly, on WebGL 2 with WebGL 1 as a fallback.
projects.nakoa.detail.role4: I disabled multiplayer in the web demo and kept the full project off GitHub because of its size; I share it by email on request.
projects.nakoa.detail.arch_intro: One project, four outputs. Unity's build pipeline produces one version per target from the same code; the WebGL one is published as a static site and is the only one without multiplayer.
projects.nakoa.detail.diagram_alt: Nakoa architecture: a single Unity project with shared scenes, C# logic and assets, the multiplayer client and a per-device input and UI layer; the build produces four targets: Android and iOS on mobile, PC on Windows, macOS and Linux, and WebGL in the browser, the only one without multiplayer.
projects.nakoa.detail.step1: A single Unity project: scenes, C# logic and assets, shared by every platform.
projects.nakoa.detail.step2: Input and UI adapt to the device, so the game feels at home on each one.
projects.nakoa.detail.step3: Unity's build pipeline produces one version per target: Android, iOS, PC on Windows, macOS and Linux, and WebGL.
projects.nakoa.detail.step4: The WebGL build runs in the browser with WebAssembly and is published on GitHub Pages, without multiplayer.
projects.nakoa.detail.learned: That cross-platform isn't pressing “Build” four times. Every target has its limits, and the browser is the strictest: you have to decide early what is shared and what depends on the device, and accept that the web demo can't do everything.
projects.telegram.detail.lead: A bot for the Telegram group of a student flat with a joint bank account. It checks the balance and transactions through Open Banking, tells who hasn't paid and takes care of the reminders nobody keeps.
projects.telegram.detail.fact2_label: banking endpoints: balances, details and transactions
projects.telegram.detail.fact3_label: automatic alerts: rent and late payers
projects.telegram.detail.fact4_label: window to spot who hasn't paid
projects.telegram.detail.context: In a flat with a joint account, money causes more arguments than the dishes: forgotten payments, balances nobody knows and reminders lost in the chat. The Telegram group was already where everything got discussed, so the bot lives there and answers with the account's real data.
projects.telegram.detail.role1: I wrote the bot in Python with python-telegram-bot: every command is an async handler and, in the group, it only replies when mentioned.
projects.telegram.detail.role2: I connected the joint account to GoCardless's Open Banking API for /saldo, /iban and /transacciones, which shows the last six transactions.
projects.telegram.detail.role3: I built /morosos: it checks the transfers of the last 20 days and tells who has paid their share and who hasn't.
projects.telegram.detail.role4: I added reminders that are saved to reminders.json and rescheduled on startup, and made the bot cope with the API's rate limit: on a 429 it says how long to wait and retries.
projects.telegram.detail.arch_intro: A single Python process listens to Telegram through long polling and runs the scheduled alerts on the same job queue. The Telegram and GoCardless tokens are passed as arguments at startup and never stored in the repository.
projects.telegram.detail.diagram_alt: Bot architecture: the flat's Telegram group sends commands to the Python bot through long polling; the bot has its command handlers, the JobQueue for alerts and reminders and the reminders.json file; it queries GoCardless's Open Banking API (balances, details and transactions), which reads the bank's joint account, and the automatic alerts go back to the group.
projects.telegram.detail.step1: Someone types a command in the group mentioning the bot, which picks it up through long polling.
projects.telegram.detail.step2: The handler calls the GoCardless API with the access token: balance, account details or transactions.
projects.telegram.detail.step3: GoCardless reads the bank's joint account through Open Banking and the bot sums up the reply in the chat.
projects.telegram.detail.step4: Reminders are scheduled on the job queue and saved to reminders.json so they survive a restart.
projects.telegram.detail.step5: Every morning the queue checks whether an alert is due: rent at the start of the month, late payers at the end.
projects.telegram.detail.learned: That a small tool gets used if it lives where people already are. And that when you depend on an external API you have to design for failure: rate limits, retries and messages that explain what's going on instead of going silent.
projects.tareas.detail.lead: An app to run a shared flat: chores split by room, a shared shopping list, reminders that notify your phone and shared expenses, all synced in real time across everyone who lives there.
projects.tareas.detail.fact2_label: tabs: home, chores, shopping and reminders
projects.tareas.detail.fact3_label: collections per flat, synced in real time
projects.tareas.detail.fact4_label: state contexts: user, group and theme
projects.tareas.detail.context: In a shared flat, chores and expenses get split over chat and forgotten just as fast. Repartir Tareas brings it all together: each flat is a group with its members, rooms, chores, shopping and bills, and whatever one person changes, the others see instantly.
projects.tareas.detail.role1: I designed and built the whole app with React Native and Expo: sign-in, four main tabs, profile and group settings.
projects.tareas.detail.role2: I modelled the data in Firestore: each group stores its chores, rooms, shopping, reminders, payments and join requests, and the app listens to every collection in real time.
projects.tareas.detail.role3: I built the room editor with gestures: drag to move, pinch to resize, twist with two fingers to rotate and double-tap to change the shape.
projects.tareas.detail.role4: I gave the owner control of the group: accepting requests, removing members, renaming it, handing over ownership or deleting it.
projects.tareas.detail.arch_intro: Three layers and no server of my own. Screens read and write through three React contexts; Firebase Authentication handles the session and Firestore is both the database and the real-time channel.
projects.tareas.detail.diagram_alt: Repartir Tareas architecture: the React Native app uses three React contexts, UserContext, GroupContext and ThemeContext; UserContext keeps the session with Firebase Authentication and GroupContext listens in real time to the group's Firestore collections and writes with transactions and batches; reminders are scheduled as notifications on the phone.
projects.tareas.detail.step1: Firebase Authentication handles sign-up, login and password recovery; UserContext keeps the user and their groups.
projects.tareas.detail.step2: On entering a flat, GroupContext opens a listener for each of the group's collections and the screens update by themselves.
projects.tareas.detail.step3: Whatever can't be left half-done goes in a transaction or a batch: the group's unique name, the change of owner and the shopping order.
projects.tareas.detail.step4: When a reminder with a future date arrives, expo-notifications schedules it on the phone and it's marked as notified.
projects.tareas.detail.stack1: React Native 0.79 and Expo SDK 53, with a development client
projects.tareas.detail.stack2: React Navigation 7: a stack for the session and bottom tabs
projects.tareas.detail.stack3: gesture-handler and Reanimated for the floor plan; draggable-flatlist to reorder the shopping list
projects.tareas.detail.learned: That in a collaborative app the hard part isn't the screens but the shared state: who can change what, and what happens if two people do it at once. Listening to the database instead of asking it simplified the whole UI.
projects.paper.detail.lead: The paper evaluates how much a chest X-ray adds to predicting, 24 hours ahead, the deterioration of ICU patients. I'm presenting it at CAEPIA 2026 in Jaén, Spain, on 11 November.
projects.paper.detail.context1: It's the research I've done during my Master's in Computer Engineering at Universidad de Sevilla, co-authored with Andreea Madalina Oprescu and María del Carmen Romero Ternero.
projects.paper.detail.context2: The question is the one in the title: what a chest X-ray contributes when you try to predict, a day in advance, which ICU patients are going to deteriorate.
projects.paper.detail.context3: CAEPIA is the conference of the Spanish Association for Artificial Intelligence (AEPIA). Its 21st edition takes place on 11–13 November 2026 at the Antigua Escuela de Magisterio of Universidad de Jaén.

method.title: How I work with AI
method.sdd.name: Spec-Driven Development
method.sdd.desc: Spec, contracts and non-negotiable decisions are written before the code; the model implements against them.
method.tdd.name: Tests first
method.tdd.desc: Pure logic in DOM-free modules, tested in Node; every fix with a test seen failing first.
method.review.name: Adversarial review
method.review.desc: Every milestone is reviewed by several agents with different lenses; each finding is verified and applied before the next one.
method.docs.name: Living docs
method.docs.desc: Tests check that the README and project map never drift from the code.
